betterCitation: Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail, 16 April 1963, the 1963 circulating text; revised for Why We Can’t Wait, ch. 5, 1964
reason: Refuted on the citation, not on the words. What I could confirm: the two sentences are consecutive and not stitched. I pulled the full text the evidence names and the paragraph runs Moreover, I am cognizant of the interrelatedness of all communities and states. I cannot sit idly by in Atlanta and not be concerned about what happens in Birmingham. Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny. Whatever affects one directly, affects all indirectly. So the sentence pair is real and in that order. What breaks it is the edition. The source line names Why We Can’t Wait, ch. 5 (Harper and Row, 1964) as the edition the wording comes from, and nobody opened it. The evidence field says so itself: where reads a full text of the letter, edition reads the standard circulating text, and the url is letterfromjail.com, an anonymous site of no stated provenance whose page even repeats the sentence once as a pull quote. That is a quotation site standing in for a named edition, which is the thing this track forbids. It matters here more than usual because the 1964 book is not a reprint. Stanford’s King Institute states plainly that one year later King revised the letter and presented it as a chapter in his 1964 memoir, and the chapter carries an author’s note the 1963 text does not. So there are at least two recensions, the source line asserts the later one, and the text checked is the earlier one. I could not reach a 1964 Harper and Row text to settle it: archive.org search inside, the petabox scrape endpoint and a page-number search all failed. I therefore cannot say the 1964 wording is identical, and under this track’s standard an unverified edition claim is a confident false citation waiting to happen. Chapter 5 itself does check out. Two further things the editor should weigh even if the 1964 page is later opened. First, copyright: this is the only line in the batch not in the public domain. The letter is under active, aggressively licensed copyright to the King estate into the 2050s, while the other three are 1838, 1843 and 1869. Twenty-four quoted words with full attribution is a strong fair use case, not a certainty, and it is the sort of exposure a shipping app should choose deliberately. Second, scope, which I raise but do not rest on: the brief gives speeches and oratory to the Makers, and this is an open letter written for public persuasion, the single most quoted passage of American civil rights rhetoric. Its form is a letter, so the Correspondence tag is defensible, but it sits closer to the Makers’ ground than anything else in the month. The betterCitation offered is provisional and honest about which text was read: it claims only the 1963 circulating text and notes the 1964 revision rather than asserting it. If the editor wants the 1964 book named, someone has to open the 1964 book.
